newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Economists rule out Thai baht devaluation.
newsitem.headline: Economists rule out Thai baht devaluation.

text.p: There is no reason why the Thai baht should be devalued, economists said on Thursday as the currency recovered in Asia after Wednesday's sell-off.

"The economic fundamentals are with the Bank of Thailand. The current account deficit is collapsing. There's no reason for a devaluation," Desmond Supple, Chief Economist Asia-Pacific at BZW in Singapore told Reuters.
Lawrence Hathaway, Chief Economist East Asia at UBS Securities in Singapore agreed. "There are sound reasons that devaluation is not unambiguously good for the economy."
At 0322 gmt the baht was quoted against the dollar at 25.80/90. Traders said there was little activity because of the huge dealing spread.
On Wednesday, the baht hit a low around 26.26, prompting joint intervention to support the currency from the Bank of Thailand and the Monetary Authority of Singapore.
Market talk also had it that other Asian central banks, such as the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, also intervened to defend the baht, but there was no confirmation.
The baht has come under speculative pressure in the last couple of days on growing concern about the slowing Thai economy and rumours of political turmoil within the Thai cabinet.
There were also rumours that Finance Minister Amnay Viravan could resign, although he has denied this.

BZW's Supple said the Bank of Thailand was fighting the speculators by pushing short-term rates sharply higher. "The implied overnight rate is at 150 percent right now. They're making the speculators pay," he said.
By boosting short-term interest rates central banks can make it hugely expensive for speculators to short a currency.
A foreign exchange dealer will short a currency -- sell currency he does not have -- in the hope the currency will be trading at a lower level when it comes time to settle the deal.
His profit is the difference between the high rate at which he sold and the low rate at which he bought the currency back.
"The Bank of Thailand's economic policies are working, but the market is trying them on," Supple said.

He said Thailand had been very successful in reducing the current account deficit. The deficit was now around six percent of Gross Domestic Product (GDP), compared with 8.2 percent last year, he said.
"If you look at the three month moving average the current account deficit was 18 billion baht in February compared with 37 billion in February last year," Supple said.
"The people forecasting devaluation are assuming the current account deficit will not come down and that's just not the case," he said.
Hathaway of UBS commented; "The Thai central bank is very committed to maintaining the current baht peg. There's been no wavering at the political level."
As Hathaway spoke to Reuters, Amnuay was in Tokyo telling an international conference, "We are determined to fight speculation. I repeat we are determined to fight speculation."
The Bank of Thailand also told investors in a statement not to listen to rumours of a devaluation. It said its intervention was meant to protect against speculation on the currency.
Hathaway said that to protect the economy, "The Thai central bank will be reluctant to boost interest rates for a prolonged period of time."
But with short-term rates moving up so sharply, "It underscores how expensive it is to short the currency."
The head of foreign currency trading at a European bank in Singapore agreed.
Referring to the rise in short-term rates, he said, "They are not going to devalue the baht and they'll go to any lengths to avoid it."
-- Singapore newsroom (65) 870-3080
